content: Natural birth control refers to methods of contraception that are considered natural, though the definition of natural can vary significantly. Typically, natural birth control excludes the use of hormonal contraceptives and synthetic chemicals, including synthetic spermicides. Depending on the interpretation of natural, other methods may also be excluded. Some definitions are more lenient and include barrier methods without synthetic spermicides, and occasionally the copper intrauterine device (IUD), which does not contain hormones. Other definitions exclude devices altogether but allow the use of herbs, natural substances, and behavioral methods. Natural family planning is the most restrictive in its definition of what constitutes natural. Methods of Natural Birth Control Fertility Tracking Fertility tracking methods, such as fertility awareness and the rhythm method, are often considered forms of natural birth control. Fertility awareness involves monitoring biological signs of fertility, such as changes in cervical mucus or basal body temperature. The rhythm method, on the other hand, uses statistical calculations based on the length of previous menstrual cycles to estimate fertile periods. Herbs and Natural Substances Some naturally occurring substances are used as alternatives to synthetic chemicals and are considered natural by some definitions. These substances may be ingested to interfere with ovulation or implantation, or they may be used to encourage menstruation. Others are applied vaginally as natural spermicides. Examples include lemon juice, wild yam, Queen Anne's Lace (wild carrot), and neem. A website called Sister Zeus provides detailed descriptions of these methods. Sexual Activity Certain sexual activities that carry no or minimal risk of conception are also considered natural birth control methods. The withdrawal method, which involves removing the penis from the vagina before ejaculation, is one of the most well-known techniques. Anal sex may be used as a substitute for vaginal intercourse. Non-penetrative sexual activities, such as oral sex, masturbation, erotic massage, the use of sex toys, and frottage, are also included in this category. Barrier Methods Without Synthetic Spermicide Barrier methods, such as condoms, female condoms, diaphragms, cervical caps, and Lea's shields, are sometimes considered natural because they do not involve hormones or systemic effects on the body. These methods work by physically blocking sperm from entering the uterus. They can be combined with natural substances, including natural spermicides, to enhance effectiveness. Miscellaneous Methods Heat-Based Contraception: This experimental method involves heating the testicles to kill sperm and temporarily inhibit sperm production. Copper IUD: The copper IUD is sometimes considered a natural method because it does not have systemic effects on the body and contains no hormones. Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM): This method extends the natural period of postpartum infertility through breastfeeding. Frequent breastfeeding maintains elevated levels of the hormone prolactin, which can suppress ovulation. Total Sexual Abstinence: Since pregnancy cannot occur without sexual activity, complete abstinence is sometimes regarded as a form of natural birth control. Natural Family Planning (NFP) Proponents of the Catholic concept of natural family planning (NFP) define natural differently. The Catholic Church approves only total or periodic abstinence and temporary infertility caused by breastfeeding as acceptable methods of family planning. NFP prohibits all orgasmic acts outside of unprotected vaginal intercourse with one's spouse, in accordance with Catholic religious beliefs. Periodic abstinence involves avoiding sexual intercourse during the fertile period around ovulation. Fertile times can be identified using fertility awareness methods, such as observing changes in cervical mucus or basal body temperature, or approximated using statistical methods like the rhythm method. Extending the natural period of breastfeeding-induced infertility through specific breastfeeding practices (LAM) is also permitted.
